transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, occupational health asked me to come in. I think they’re being a bit dramatic, but… I have gotten into this routine where I just sort of push breakfast and lunch aside when I’m in the lab or caught up with exhibition work. You know how lab runs can be—once you start, it’s hard to stop, and there’s always one more thing to check.

And then by the time I do eat, I keep it very small. Controlled, I suppose. It’s just become a pattern, and they seemed concerned about it.
Do you ever feel anxious about gaining weight or have specific concerns about your body shape or size?

Yes… I mean, I don’t like admitting that, because it sounds irrational when I say it out loud. But if the scale goes up even a tiny bit, even a fraction, I get this sudden sharp panic, like I’ve somehow lost control or lost the discipline I’ve worked so hard to keep.

It’s strange, because in the lab I’m very used to small variations meaning nothing—noise in the data, calibration issues, that sort of thing—but with my own weight I don’t seem to treat it that way. I just… react.
Do you ever engage in behaviors like excessive exercise, making yourself vomit, or using laxatives or diet pills to manage your weight or shape?

I… don’t really know how to answer that neatly. I mean, I do think a lot about control, obviously, and routines, but the vomiting or laxatives or diet pills—that’s not really something I’ve got a clear thing to tell you about.

Exercise is a bit harder to define, isn’t it? Because some people call anything excessive now. I walk around the museum a lot, and the lab is constant back-and-forth—though actually the new storage layout is ridiculous, they put the specimen drawers so far from the imaging room that everyone’s steps have probably doubled. But I don’t know if that’s what you mean.

So… I’m not sure. I haven’t really thought of myself as doing those specific things to manage my weight.

When you think about your activity levels, do you ever feel driven to move or exercise specifically to control your weight or shape, even if it's not what you'd call traditional exercise like going to a gym?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean, I do move around a lot, but it’s sort of built into the day—between the lab, the museum spaces, carrying things, going back for keys I’ve inevitably left somewhere. Honestly the key situation is absurd; I’ve thought about putting them on one of those retractable cords, but then I’d look like a caretaker.

Sorry, that’s not really what you asked. I don’t know that I think, “I must exercise to change my shape,” if that makes sense. Sometimes I do feel better if I’m not just sitting still, but whether that’s about weight or just restlessness or habit… I’m not entirely sure.
When you choose not to eat or keep your meals small, is it primarily to prevent gaining weight or to lose weight?

Yes… I think so. I don’t usually say it as plainly as “I’m doing this to lose weight,” because that sounds very deliberate, almost like a plan written in a lab notebook or something. But if I’m honest, keeping meals small feels safer because the idea of the scale going up—even just a tiny fraction—sets off this horrible panic.

It’s not even a rational amount, you know? In any other context I’d say a fraction is meaningless. But with me, it feels like I’m losing control, or losing the discipline I’ve been trying so hard to maintain. So… yes, I suppose it’s mostly about preventing that.
Do you feel that your weight or shape has more influence on how you see yourself than it should—like it's more important than other parts of who you are?

Yes… probably more than it should. I don’t like admitting that, because I know there are other things I’m supposed to value about myself—my work, whether I’m careful in the lab, whether I’m useful to people.

But in the morning, before I go in, if I catch myself in the mirror, I don’t see someone thin. I just sort of zero in on my stomach or my hips, and then it feels like they say something about me, like I look careless or unserious. Which is absurd, really, because no one at the lab is judging my competence by that—I mean, they’re usually more concerned about whether the freezer alarm is going off again. But it feels that way to me. Like my shape somehow becomes evidence against me.
Do you believe that your concerns about your weight or shape are stronger or more influential than they should be, even if you can't quite control how you feel about them?

Yes… I do think they’re stronger than they should be. I can know, intellectually, that it’s ridiculous—like, no one is standing at the lab bench evaluating my stomach or my hips before deciding whether I’m competent with a sample. They’re usually asking if I’ve seen the pipettes or if the incubator is making that odd clicking noise again.

But when I look in the mirror before work, I don’t see someone thin or even just… normal. I immediately focus on those parts, and they feel like they mean something about me. Like they make me look careless, or unserious somehow. I don’t want them to have that much say in how I feel about myself, but they do.
How often do you find yourself skipping or reducing meals because of concerns about your weight or shape—nearly every day, several times a week, or less often?

Nearly every day, I suppose. I mean, not always in a dramatic way where I announce I’m skipping a meal or anything. It’s more that I get into a lab run, or there’s exhibition work to sort through, and breakfast gets pushed aside… then lunch gets pushed aside too.

And then by the time I do eat, I make it very small, very controlled. Occupational health seemed to think that pattern was enough of a problem to send me here, which… I suppose is fair, even if part of me wants to say it’s just because the day gets busy. But it isn’t only that.
Do you feel that your body weight or shape is experienced differently than it actually is—like perceiving yourself as larger than you are?

Yes… I think so. Not exactly like I’m hallucinating or anything, but when I look in the mirror before I go to the lab, I don’t really see someone thin. I just go straight to my stomach or my hips, and they seem… bigger, or more wrong, than they probably are.

And then I start thinking they make me look careless, or unserious, which is silly because in the lab no one cares—well, except if you’ve mislabeled a tube, then everyone cares very much. But my mind turns my shape into this kind of evidence about me, even though I know that doesn’t really make sense.
Do these concerns about your eating, weight, or shape interfere with your work, relationships, or other important areas of your life?

Yes… somewhat. I’m still getting the main work done, I think. Deadlines are being met, samples processed, the necessary emails sent—though honestly, email threads about shared freezer space could drive anyone into a cave.

But I have stopped going to things like lab lunches. And there are these informal meals around gallery planning sometimes, where people talk through ideas over food, and I used to go because that’s where a lot of the useful conversation happens. Now I tend to make an excuse or say I have something to finish.

So… I’m not failing at work, exactly, but I’m more separate from people than I used to be. More on the outside of things.
Have you ever had episodes where you feel like you’re eating in a way that’s out of control—like eating a lot in a short time or feeling unable to stop—even if it’s not something you do often?

I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t think I have a clear example in mind of, you know, sitting down and suddenly not being able to stop in that way.

I suppose I get confused by what counts as “a lot,” because people in the lab will say they’ve eaten loads when they’ve had, like, two biscuits during a meeting, and then someone else brings in those enormous supermarket muffins and calls it a snack. Sorry, that’s not really the point.

I haven’t really noticed episodes like that, no—not in a way I’d know how to describe as out of control.

Have you ever tried to compensate for eating by restricting even further, exercising more, or doing anything else specifically to undo the effects of food—even if it wasn’t in a clear episode of overeating?

I suppose… yes, in a way. Not like a formal “I ate this, therefore I must do that” kind of calculation, or at least I don’t think of it that neatly.

It’s more that occupational health sent me because I’ve got into this pattern where I push breakfast and lunch aside during lab runs, or when I’m helping with exhibition work, and then by the time I do eat I keep it very small and controlled.

Sometimes I tell myself it’s just because the timing is awkward—because experiments don’t pause politely for lunch, which honestly they should, if cells had any manners at all—but I think part of it is also that if I’ve eaten something, I feel like I need to make the next thing smaller. Or delay it. So yes, I suppose restricting further is probably the main thing.

Have your concerns about eating, weight, or shape caused you significant distress or affected your ability to function in any important areas of your life, such as your relationships, work performance, or participation in social activities?

Yes… I mean, I’m still functioning on paper. The main deadlines are still getting done, and I don’t think anyone could say I’ve dropped the ball at work exactly.

But socially, yes, it’s changed things. I’ve stopped going to lab lunches, and those informal gallery planning meals where people sort of talk through ideas while eating—I used to go to those. Sometimes that’s where the useful conversations happen, not in the actual meetings, which is annoying but true.

Now I tend to make some excuse, like I’ve got something to finish or I need to check something in the lab. And then I’m just… not there. So I’m more cut off from colleagues than I used to be. More isolated, I suppose.
Do you typically restrict your eating in response to specific concerns about your weight or shape, even when you haven’t eaten in an out-of-control way?

Yes, I think so. I mean, it’s not usually after some out-of-control eating thing. It’s more… I’ve got into this pattern where during lab runs, or if I’m doing exhibition work, I just push breakfast and lunch aside.

And then later, when I do eat, I keep it very small and controlled. I tell myself it’s because the timing’s awkward—experiments don’t really care whether you’ve had lunch—but yes, it does connect to worries about eating and keeping things contained.

Now I tend to make some excuse, like I’ve got something to finish or I need to check something in the lab. And then I’m just… not there. So I’m more cut off from colleagues than I used to be. More isolated, I suppose.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's restrictive eating behaviors occur independently of binge eating episodes, to differentiate between anorexia nervosa (F50.01) and bulimia nervosa (F50.2).
doctor.question: Do you typically restrict your eating in response to specific concerns about your weight or shape, even when you haven’t eaten in an out-of-control way?

target_item.name: Restrictive_Intake
target_item.manifestation: I suppose occupational health sent me because I’ve gotten into this pattern where I push breakfast and lunch aside during lab runs or exhibition work and then, by the time I eat, I keep it to something very small and controlled.
target_item.reason: The question is most directly asking about the pattern of restricting eating, even when it is not in response to out-of-control eating.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think so. I mean, it’s not usually after some out-of-control eating thing. It’s more… I’ve got into this pattern where during lab runs, or if I’m doing exhibition work, I just push breakfast and lunch aside.

And then later, when I do eat, I keep it very small and controlled. I tell myself it’s because the timing’s awkward—experiments don’t really care whether you’ve had lunch—but yes, it does connect to worries about eating and keeping things contained.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets diagnostic criteria for Anorexia Nervosa, characterized by restrictive eating behaviors in response to concerns about weight and shape, intense fear of gaining weight, body image disturbance, and associated functional impairment in social and occupational domains. There is no evidence of recurrent binge eating or compensatory behaviors like purging, which makes F50.2 (Atypical Anorexia Nervosa) less fitting.
